blocks.text: Introduction about health

Most people think of health as simply the absence of disease, but this is an incomplete view. Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. When people are healthy they are more efficient at work, which increases productivity and brings economic prosperity. Health also reduces the infant and maternal mortality in a population. Good health therefore depends on more than medicine.
A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

Three broad groups of factors influence health. **Genetic disorders** are present from birth and can be inherited. **Infections** are caused by disease-causing organisms, the pathogens. **Lifestyle**, including food and water, rest and exercise, habits and addictions, also decides health. Balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise are important, and so are yoga and meditation. Awareness about diseases, vaccination against infectious diseases, proper disposal of wastes, control of vectors and maintenance of hygienic food and water sources are the means to prevent infectious diseases. A disease is called **infectious** if it spreads from one person to another, and **non-infectious** if it does not, as in cancer.
Common diseases in humans

Pathogens are the organisms that cause disease and may be bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans or helminths. They enter the body by air, water, food, vectors or contact, multiply inside host tissues, and damage the host. The common diseases in the syllabus are described below.

**Typhoid** is caused by the bacterium *Salmonella typhi*, which enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and then reaches other organs through the blood. Symptoms are sustained high fever (39 to 40 degrees Celsius), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite. Intestinal perforation and death may occur in severe cases. The disease is confirmed by the **Widal test**.

**Pneumonia** is caused by bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*, which infect the alveoli of the lungs. The alveoli get filled with fluid, which leads to severe problems in respiration. Symptoms are fever, chills, cough and headache, and in severe cases the lips and finger nails turn gray to bluish. It spreads by droplets or aerosols released by an infected person, and also by sharing glasses and utensils.

**Common cold** is caused by rhinoviruses, which infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. The symptoms are nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache and tiredness, usually lasting for 3 to 7 days. The droplets from the cough or sneeze of an infected person are inhaled, or enter through contaminated objects such as pens, books and door handles.

**Malaria** is caused by the protozoan *Plasmodium*. The species that infect man are *P. vivax*, *P. malariae* and *P. falciparum*, and the most serious, which can be fatal, is **malignant malaria** caused by *P. falciparum*. The female *Anopheles* mosquito is the vector. When it bites, it injects the infectious stage, the **sporozoites**, into the blood. The sporozoites multiply in the liver cells and then attack the red blood cells (RBCs), which burst and release a toxin called **haemozoin**. This is responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. Gametocytes formed in RBCs are taken up by a mosquito, where fertilisation and development take place, and the sporozoites reach its salivary glands, ready to infect another person.

**Amoebiasis** (amoebic dysentery) is caused by the protozoan *Entamoeba histolytica*, a parasite of the large intestine. Symptoms are constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, and stools with excess mucus and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers and serve to transmit the parasite from faeces to food, and the disease spreads through contaminated food and drinking water.

**Ascariasis** is caused by the intestinal roundworm *Ascaris*. Symptoms include internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage. The eggs of the parasite are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons, and they contaminate soil, water, plants, vegetables and fruits. Infection is by ingesting the contaminated food or water.

**Filariasis** (elephantiasis) is caused by filarial worms such as *Wuchereria bancrofti* and *W. malayi*. They live in the lymphatic vessels, mostly of the lower limbs, and cause a slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs in which they live. Gross deformities of the limbs and genital organs may result. The filarial worms are transmitted to a healthy person through the bite of the female *Culex* mosquito vector.

**Ringworm** is caused by fungi of the genera *Microsporum*, *Trichophyton* and *Epidermophyton*. They infect the skin, nails and scalp, producing dry, scaly lesions on various parts of the body with intense itching. Heat and moisture help these fungi to grow, and they thrive in skin folds such as the groin and between the toes. The infection spreads from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected persons.

blocks.text: **Prevention and control.** Personal hygiene means keeping the body clean, and using clean drinking water, food and vegetables. Public hygiene means proper disposal of waste and excreta, periodic cleaning of water reservoirs, and control of the vectors. For vector-borne diseases, avoid stagnation of water in and around residences, regularly clean coolers, use mosquito nets, introduce larvivorous fish like *Gambusia* in ponds, spray insecticides in ditches and drains, and fit doors and windows with wire mesh. *Aedes* mosquitoes spread dengue and chikungunya.
Immunity: innate and acquired, active and passive
The ability of the host to fight the disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system.

**Innate immunity** is non-specific and present at the time of birth. It consists of four types of barriers. **Physical barriers** include the skin and the mucus coating of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts, which traps microbes. **Physiological barriers** include acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth and tears from the eyes. **Cellular barriers** are the leucocytes such as neutrophils (PMNL), monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes and macrophages, which phagocytose and destroy microbes. **Cytokine barriers** are formed by proteins such as **interferons**, secreted by virus-infected cells, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

**Acquired immunity** is pathogen-specific and is characterised by **memory**. When the body encounters a pathogen for the first time, it produces a **primary response** of low intensity. A second encounter with the same pathogen produces a **secondary (anamnestic) response** that is highly intensified, because the body remembers the first encounter. The primary and secondary responses are carried out by two special types of lymphocytes, the **B-lymphocytes** and **T-lymphocytes**. B cells produce proteins in response to pathogens, called **antibodies**, which fight the pathogens. T cells themselves do not secrete antibodies but help B cells to produce them.

An antibody molecule has four peptide chains, two small **light chains** and two longer **heavy chains**, so it is written H2L2. Different types of antibodies are produced in our body, such as IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG. The B cell response is called the **humoral immune response (HIR)**, because the antibodies are in the body fluids. The second is the **cell-mediated immune response (CMI)**, carried out by T cells. This system lets the body differentiate between self and non-self, so CMI is responsible for graft rejection. In organ transplantation, the tissue matching and blood group matching and immunosuppressants are used to prevent the rejection.

**Active immunity** is produced when a host is exposed to antigens, which may be live or inactivated pathogens or proteins of pathogens. The host's own antibodies are made, and the response is slow and takes time to give its full effect. **Passive immunity** is produced when readymade antibodies are given directly to protect the body against foreign agents. For example, the yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant, and the foetus receives some antibodies (IgG) from the mother through the placenta.

blocks.text: Vaccination and immunisation

**Vaccination** works on the principle of the memory of the immune system. A preparation of inactivated or weakened pathogens, or of their proteins, called a **vaccine**, is introduced into the body. The antibodies produced in response neutralise the pathogenic agents during actual infection, and the vaccine also generates memory B and T cells that recognise the pathogen quickly on a later contact and destroy it with a massive production of antibodies. Vaccines for polio, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and others are available.

In emergencies such as a snake bite, the injection of preformed antibodies, **antivenom**, is given, and in tetanus an injection of **antitoxin**, which gives passive immunity. Recombinant DNA technology has made vaccine production possible in bacteria or yeast, for example the hepatitis B vaccine from yeast. **Immunisation** is the process of making an individual immune, and it includes vaccination and the giving of readymade antibodies.

blocks.problem: A child is given the polio vaccine. Months later another child is bitten by a venomous snake and is given antivenom. State the type of immunity in each case, whether memory forms, and why the antivenom works faster.
blocks.solution: The polio vaccine contains weakened or inactivated antigens, so the child's own B and T cells respond and make antibodies and memory cells. This is active immunity, and it is slow but long lasting, and memory forms. The antivenom is a preparation of readymade antibodies, so the second child does not make them. This is passive immunity. It acts immediately because the antibodies are already present, but no memory cells are formed in the receiver, so protection is short-lived.
blocks.answer: Vaccine: active immunity with memory; antivenom: passive immunity, immediate, no memory

blocks.text: Allergies, auto-immunity and the immune system in human

**Allergy** is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment, called **allergens**, such as dust, pollen and mites. The antibodies produced against allergens are of the IgE type. Allergens trigger **mast cells** to release **histamine** and serotonin, which cause the symptoms of sneezing, watery eyes, a running nose and difficulty in breathing. Drugs like anti-histamine, adrenaline and steroids quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy. The cause of such sensitivity is not clearly understood, but modern lifestyle with protection from many allergens in early childhood is thought to contribute.

**Auto-immunity** occurs when the memory-based acquired immunity attacks the body's own cells because the immune system fails to distinguish self from non-self. This causes damage to the body and is called an auto-immune disease. **Rheumatoid arthritis** is an example.

The **immune system** consists of lymphoid organs, tissues, cells and soluble molecules like antibodies. **Primary lymphoid organs** are the **bone marrow** and the **thymus**, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes. Bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells are produced. The thymus is a lobed organ near the heart, large at birth but reducing in size with age. After maturation, the lymphocytes migrate to **secondary lymphoid organs** such as the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and the appendix, where they interact with the antigen and become effector cells. The spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that mainly contains lymphocytes and phagocytes, and it filters blood. **Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)** lies in the lining of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts and constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.
AIDS
Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome: a deficiency of the immune system that is acquired during the lifetime and not inherited, caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).

HIV is a **retrovirus** with an RNA genome. It spreads through sexual contact with an infected person, through transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products, by sharing infected needles as among intravenous drug users, and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. HIV is **not** spread by touching or sitting together, or by the sharing of clothes or food. People at high risk are those with multiple sexual partners, drug addicts who use intravenous needles, individuals who need repeated blood transfusions, and children born to an HIV-infected mother.

After entering the body, the virus enters **macrophages**, where its RNA genome is converted to viral DNA by the enzyme **reverse transcriptase**. The viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cells to produce virus particles. The macrophages continue to produce virus and thus act as an HIV factory. Meanwhile, HIV enters **helper T-lymphocytes (TH)**, replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack other helper T cells. The number of TH cells progressively decreases, and the person becomes immune-deficient, suffering from infections of bacteria, especially *Mycobacterium*, viruses, fungi and the parasite *Toxoplasma*, and cannot defend against even minor infections.

The diagnostic test widely used is **ELISA** (enzyme-linked immuno-sorbent assay). Treatment with antiretroviral drugs is only partially effective, so prevention is the best option. Prevention involves making blood from safe, HIV-free donors available, using disposable needles and syringes, free distribution of condoms, controlling drug abuse, advocating safe sex, and regular check-ups. The National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) and other NGOs educate people about AIDS.
Cancer

Normal cells show a property called **contact inhibition**, by which contact with other cells inhibits uncontrolled growth. **Cancer cells** have lost this property, so they divide continuously and form a mass of cells called a **tumour**. A **benign tumour** remains confined to the place of origin, causes little damage and does not spread. A **malignant tumour** is a mass of proliferating cells called neoplastic or tumour cells, which grow very rapidly, invade and damage the surrounding normal tissues. Cells sloughed from such tumours reach other sites through blood and wherever they lodge, they start a new tumour. This spread is called **metastasis**, and it makes malignant tumours dangerous.

Agents that cause cancer are **carcinogens**. They may be physical (ionising radiations such as X-rays and gamma rays, and non-ionising UV rays), chemical (tobacco smoke is the main cause of lung cancer) or biological (cancer-causing viruses called **oncogenic viruses**, which have genes called viral oncogenes). Normal cells contain genes called **cellular oncogenes** or **proto-oncogenes**, which, when activated under certain conditions, lead to oncogenic transformation.

**Detection and diagnosis** is by biopsy and histopathological study of the tissue, blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in leukaemia, and by radiography, CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens, and techniques of molecular biology to detect genes, are used. **Treatment** includes surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Many chemotherapeutic drugs have side effects like hair loss and anaemia. **Immunotherapy** uses biological response modifiers such as **alpha-interferon**, which activate the immune system and help in destroying the tumour.
Drugs and alcohol abuse: adolescence, addiction, effects, prevention and control

**Adolescence** is the period between about 12 and 18 years of age and a bridge between childhood and adulthood. It is a period of rapid physical and psychological change, curiosity and experimentation, and it is also the age at which many begin to use drugs and alcohol. Curiosity, the wish to experiment, stress, peer pressure, family problems, the influence of films and media, and the false belief that drugs improve performance are the common reasons.

Common drugs of abuse are **opioids**, **cannabinoids** and **coca alkaloids**. Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors present in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. **Heroin**, commonly called smack, is chemically diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of **morphine**, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant *Papaver somniferum*. It is taken by snorting and injection, and it is a depressant that slows down body functions. Cannabinoids interact with cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. Natural cannabinoids are obtained from the inflorescences of the plant *Cannabis sativa*, and marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja are prepared from them. They affect the cardiovascular system of the body. **Cocaine** is obtained from the coca plant *Erythroxylum coca*. It interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, and in large doses it causes hallucinations. Other plants such as *Atropa belladonna* and *Datura* have hallucinogenic properties. Tobacco contains nicotine, which stimulates the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate.

A psychological attachment to the effects of a drug, such as euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being. With repeated use the tolerance level of the receptors increases, so larger doses are needed, and the person becomes dependent.

**Dependence** is the tendency of the body to manifest a characteristic and unpleasant **withdrawal syndrome** if the regular dose of the drug or alcohol is abruptly discontinued. Its symptoms are anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating, and it can even be life-threatening, so the user keeps taking the substance. The **effects of drug abuse** include reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence, and an **overdose** may lead to coma and death due to respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage. Use of injected drugs with shared needles spreads AIDS and hepatitis B. Drugs damage the nervous system, and alcohol over a long period damages the liver (cirrhosis). Taking alcohol with other drugs is especially dangerous, and use during adolescence can affect the mental and social development. Sportspersons sometimes misuse **anabolic steroids** to increase muscle power, and this has side effects: in males, mood swings, acne, depression, decreased testicular size, reduced sperm production, premature baldness and enlarged prostate; in females, masculinisation, increased aggressiveness, abnormal menstrual cycles and excessive hair growth on the face and body, and deepening of the voice.

**Prevention and control.** Avoid undue peer pressure, because each child is unique and should not be forced to do what others do. Educating and counselling helps children to face problems and stresses and to accept disappointments. Seek help from parents and peers, and look for danger signs: a sudden drop in academic performance, unexplained absence from school, withdrawal from family and friends, loss of interest in hobbies, changes in sleeping and eating patterns, aggressiveness, fluctuations in energy levels, deteriorating personal hygiene, lying and stealing, and an increased need for money. Professional and medical help from psychologists, psychiatrists, and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes help a user to overcome the problem.

blocks.problem: A schoolboy of 16 who was a good student is now often absent without explanation, avoids his family, sleeps at odd hours, has lost interest in sports and asks his parents for extra money. Using the syllabus, state what the signs suggest and list the steps that his parents and teachers should take.
blocks.solution: The sudden drop in performance, unexplained absence, withdrawal from the family, changed sleeping habits, loss of interest in hobbies and the extra need for money are the standard danger signs of drug or alcohol abuse in an adolescent. The first step is a calm, non-judgemental talk, without punishment, so he does not hide the problem. The next steps are guidance and counselling to deal with peer pressure and stress, and referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist. If he is dependent, a de-addiction and rehabilitation programme should be used, with continued support, because withdrawal can be severe.
blocks.answer: Danger signs of abuse; counselling and professional medical help, de-addiction and rehabilitation

blocks.text: Quick revision: typhoid (Salmonella typhi, Widal test); pneumonia (alveoli); common cold (rhinovirus, not lungs); malaria (Plasmodium, female Anopheles, haemozoin); filariasis (lymphatic vessels, Culex); HIV (retrovirus, reverse transcriptase, helper T cells, ELISA); cancer (loss of contact inhibition, metastasis); heroin (Papaver somniferum, depressant), cocaine (Erythroxylum coca, dopamine), cannabinoids (Cannabis sativa).

Common mistakes: confusing active and passive immunity (vaccines give active; antivenom, antitoxin and colostrum give passive); saying that the common cold affects the lungs; writing that HIV spreads by touch or shared food; mixing up the source plants of heroin, cocaine and cannabinoids; and saying that the gametocyte stage of Plasmodium is the one injected by the mosquito, when the infectious stage is the sporozoite.

questions.stem: Typhoid, caused by Salmonella typhi, is confirmed by which diagnostic test?
questions.explanation: Typhoid is a bacterial disease caused by Salmonella typhi, which spreads through contaminated food and water. Its diagnosis is by the Widal test, which detects the antibodies against the bacterium in the patient's blood. ELISA is for AIDS and biopsy is for cancer.

optionRationale.2: ELISA is used to detect HIV infection, not typhoid.
optionRationale.3: Biopsy is used in the diagnosis of cancer.
optionRationale.4: This tests for tuberculosis exposure, not typhoid.

questions.objective: Name the confirmatory test for typhoid

questions.stem: The yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by a mother during the initial days of lactation provides the infant with
questions.explanation: Colostrum contains abundant ready-made antibodies, mainly IgA, which protect the infant. Since the antibodies are received from the mother and not produced by the infant's own immune system, this is passive immunity.

optionRationale.1: The infant does not make these antibodies; they are supplied ready-made.
optionRationale.3: Interferons are cytokine barriers made by virus-infected cells, not the content of colostrum.
optionRationale.4: Colostrum is not a vaccine; it carries antibodies, not antigens.

questions.objective: Classify the immunity conferred by colostrum

questions.stem: The enzyme that HIV uses to make DNA from its RNA genome is
questions.explanation: HIV is a retrovirus. After entering a host cell, its RNA is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase. The viral DNA then integrates into the host genome and directs the cell to make new virus particles.

optionRationale.1: This is a bacterial enzyme and does not convert RNA to DNA in HIV.
optionRationale.2: RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template, which is the opposite direction.
optionRationale.4: Ligase joins DNA fragments and does not make DNA from RNA.

questions.objective: Name the enzyme used by HIV for replication

questions.stem: Match List-I (disease) with List-II (causative organism) and choose the correct code.
questions.explanation: Ringworm is a fungal disease caused by Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton (A-III). Filariasis is caused by the filarial worm Wuchereria (B-IV). Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium (C-I). Ascariasis is caused by the roundworm Ascaris (D-II).

optionRationale.1: B and C are interchanged: filariasis is caused by Wuchereria and malaria by Plasmodium.
optionRationale.2: A and C are interchanged: ringworm is a fungal disease.
optionRationale.3: C and D are interchanged: Ascaris causes ascariasis.

questions.stem: The infective stage of Plasmodium that the female Anopheles mosquito injects into the human blood is the
questions.explanation: When an infected female Anopheles bites, it injects sporozoites with its saliva. They multiply in the liver cells and then invade the RBCs. The gametocytes, which develop in RBCs, are taken up by a mosquito to continue the cycle.

optionRationale.2: Gametocytes are formed in RBCs and are taken up by the mosquito; they are not the infective stage for humans.
optionRationale.3: Merozoites are formed in the liver or RBCs and attack RBCs; the mosquito does not inject them.
optionRationale.4: This is a feeding stage inside the host cells, not the stage injected by the mosquito.

questions.objective: Identify the infective stage of Plasmodium

questions.stem: An antibody molecule is made of
options: two peptide chains: one light and one heavy
four peptide chains: two light chains and two heavy chains
three peptide chains: two heavy and one light
questions.explanation: Antibodies are proteins, and each has two small light chains and two longer heavy chains, so it is represented as H2L2. IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are the main types.

optionRationale.1: The molecule has four chains, not two.
optionRationale.2: The molecule has two light and two heavy chains, not four heavy ones.
optionRationale.4: The antibody is symmetrical, with two of each chain type.

questions.objective: State the structure of an antibody

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about acquired immunity.
A. The primary response is of low intensity.
B. The secondary response is highly intensified because of memory.
C. Vaccination provides passive immunity.
D. T cells themselves secrete antibodies.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: At the first encounter with a pathogen, the response is slow and of low intensity (A). On the second encounter, memory B and T cells give a faster, stronger response (B). Vaccination produces active immunity, and antibodies are secreted by B cells, not T cells.

optionRationale.1: C is wrong: a vaccine stimulates the person's own immune system, which is active immunity.
optionRationale.3: D is wrong: T cells help B cells to produce antibodies but do not secrete them.
optionRationale.4: Both C and D are incorrect.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on primary and secondary immune response

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A person bitten by a venomous snake is given an injection of antivenom and gets immunity at once.
Reason (R): The antivenom contains readymade antibodies, so the person does not need to produce them.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Antivenom consists of preformed antibodies, which immediately neutralise the venom, so the immunity is passive and rapid. The speed of protection results directly from the fact that the antibodies need not be made by the patient, so R is the correct explanation of A.

optionRationale.2: R is the exact reason for the speed, not just a related truth.
optionRationale.3: R is true: antivenom is a readymade antibody preparation.
optionRationale.4: A is true: protection is immediate.

questions.objective: Explain why passive immunisation is immediate

questions.stem: Which property do normal cells show that cancer cells have lost?
questions.explanation: Normal cells stop growing and dividing when they touch neighbouring cells; this regulatory property is called contact inhibition. Cancer cells have lost this property, so they keep dividing without control, pile up on one another and form a tumour mass that may invade other tissues.

optionRationale.1: Both normal and cancer cells divide; the difference is the control of division.
optionRationale.3: This is not a defined property that distinguishes cancer cells in the syllabus.

questions.objective: Recall the property lost in cancer cells

questions.stem: Which of the following gives the correct sequence of events after HIV enters the body?
options: Entry into helper T cell, DNA converted to RNA, host DNA enters virus, macrophage destroyed, antibodies increase
Entry into macrophage, RNA converted to DNA by reverse transcriptase, viral DNA joins host DNA, new virus released, helper T cells infected and decrease
Entry into macrophage, viral DNA joins host DNA, RNA converted to DNA by reverse transcriptase, new virus released, helper T cells decrease
Entry into red blood cell, RNA converted to DNA, new virus released, B cells decrease
questions.explanation: HIV first enters macrophages. Reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA from the RNA genome, which then integrates into the host DNA. Infected macrophages release new viruses, and the virus then enters helper T cells, whose number progressively decreases, leading to immune deficiency.

optionRationale.1: This describes no real event in the infection.
optionRationale.3: Reverse transcription must come before integration, because the viral genome is RNA at first.
optionRationale.4: HIV does not infect red blood cells, and it is the helper T cells whose number falls.

questions.objective: Arrange the events of HIV infection in order

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A vaccinated person shows a faster and stronger response when exposed to the real pathogen.
Reason (R): Vaccination gives the person readymade antibodies against the pathogen.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Vaccination introduces weakened or inactivated antigens, so the person's own B and T cells respond and memory cells are formed. On a real infection the memory cells give a rapid and intense secondary response. So A is true. R is false, because readymade antibodies are given in passive immunisation, not in vaccination.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation.
optionRationale.2: R is false; vaccination does not supply antibodies.
optionRationale.4: A is true: memory gives the faster response.

questions.objective: Distinguish memory-based vaccination from antibody injection

questions.stem: Match List-I (drug) with List-II (plant source) and choose the correct code.
questions.explanation: Morphine is extracted from the latex of the poppy Papaver somniferum, and heroin is made from it (A-III). Cocaine is a coca alkaloid from Erythroxylum coca (B-IV). Marijuana and hashish are prepared from Cannabis sativa (C-I). Atropa belladonna is a source of hallucinogens (D-II).

optionRationale.1: A and B are interchanged: morphine comes from the poppy and cocaine from the coca plant.
optionRationale.2: C and D are interchanged: cannabinoids come from Cannabis sativa.
optionRationale.3: A and C are interchanged: marijuana is from Cannabis and morphine from the poppy.

questions.objective: Match drugs with their plant sources

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the human immune system.
A. Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs.
B. Spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils are secondary lymphoid organs.
C. Lymphocytes mature in the secondary lymphoid organs before they migrate to the primary ones.
D. MALT constitutes about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue of the body.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes mature. After maturation, they migrate to secondary organs such as the spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils, where they meet antigens. MALT in the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts is about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue. Statement C reverses the direction.

optionRationale.2: D is also correct, so this answer is incomplete.
optionRationale.3: A is correct but is omitted, and C is reversed.
optionRationale.4: B is correct but is omitted, and C is reversed.

questions.stem: A patient has high fever with chills recurring every three to four days, and the doctor finds that the infection is the most dangerous, often fatal form. Which pathogen and which toxin are responsible?
questions.explanation: The most serious form, malignant malaria, is caused by Plasmodium falciparum. When infected red blood cells burst, they release the toxin haemozoin, which causes the characteristic chills and high fever recurring every three to four days.

optionRationale.1: P. vivax causes a milder form of malaria, not the fatal malignant malaria.
optionRationale.3: Salmonella causes typhoid, and haemozoin is not its product.
optionRationale.4: Wuchereria causes filariasis; histamine is released in allergy, not in this disease.

questions.objective: Apply knowledge of malaria to a clinical description

questions.stem: Interferons secreted by virus-infected cells, which protect non-infected cells from viral infection, are part of which barrier of innate immunity?
questions.explanation: Innate immunity has physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers. Interferons are proteins released by virus-infected cells, and they protect other, non-infected cells from further viral infection. This is a chemical-signal defence, which makes them cytokine barriers rather than physical, physiological or cellular ones.

optionRationale.1: Skin and mucus are physical barriers.
optionRationale.2: Gastric acid, saliva and tears are physiological barriers.
optionRationale.4: Leucocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages are cellular barriers.
